domain_title: Health, Human Capacity, and Community Care
research_domain_title: Constitutional Health System, Rural Capacity Financing, and Prevention Dividends
note: Major national and Arkansas-ready doctrine. Healthcare is human-capital infrastructure, not merely an insurance product. Does not require government ownership of every clinic or elimination of private insurance. Financing formulas, readiness budgets, and Primary Care Floor percentages require modeling — not locked law. Legal drafting and modeling remain 0%. Sourced CMS/HRSA/CDC/ACHI baselines support problem diagnosis; architecture ≠ evidence that the Constitutional Health System already exists.

governing_principle.text: Every person must have reliable access to essential healthcare because a healthy population is foundational to liberty, productivity, family stability, community prosperity, and national strength. The system should reward keeping people healthy, restoring them quickly when sick, and delivering care as close to home as safely possible.

public_promise.text: No Arkansan should be condemned to poorer health because of their ZIP code, income, employment status, or distance from a major hospital. We will fund the capacity to keep communities healthy—not merely the transactions generated after people become sick.

doctrine_statement.text: Healthcare is a shared foundation of freedom and prosperity. The republic shall guarantee access to essential care, finance rural readiness rather than illness volume alone, reward prevention and restoration, protect medical choice and innovation, and distribute resources according to human need rather than geographic profitability.

guiding_rule.text: Basic health security follows the person. Supplemental choice may follow the market.

problem_diagnosis.summary: The present structure often pays most reliably for billable illness transactions, while rural communities need financing for permanent capacity. Volume-based incentives are especially damaging where population cannot generate urban-level admissions.
problem_diagnosis.financing_contrast: The system is financing transactions, while rural communities need financing for permanent capacity.

sourced_baselines.text: CMS operates value-based programs that reward quality of care for people with Medicare as part of reforming how care is delivered and paid for — a transition that remains incomplete relative to volume-based incentives.
According to HRSA, 152 rural hospitals closed between 2010 and 2025 (including Critical Access Hospitals among them).

CDC reports that ninety percent of the nation’s $5.3 trillion in annual health care expenditures are for people with chronic and mental health conditions — not a claim that ninety percent of spending is solely treatment of those conditions.
ACHI reports, citing Milbank Memorial Fund analysis, that 18% of Arkansas adults report not having a usual source of care — nearly 1 in 5 Arkansans.
CMS maintains distinct Critical Access Hospital and Rural Emergency Hospital frameworks for rural facility payment and emergency/outpatient preservation.

Arkansas Department of Health Primary Care Office publishes student loan repayment and scholarship programs (including HRSA and VA initiatives) aimed at reducing financial barriers for health professionals serving underserved communities.

layers.title: Universal essential-health foundation
layers.summary: A clearly defined essential package that follows the person — not lost because of job change, entrepreneurship, moves, temporary unemployment, reduced hours, leaving military service, retirement, or return from incarceration.
private_insurance_may_remain_for: additional coverage beyond the public foundation

layers.title: Shared healthcare contribution
layers.summary: Essential system funded through a broad Health and Human Capacity Contribution — not primarily premiums that punish hiring or wages. Exact formula requires economic modeling.
funding_sources_examples: corporations based partly on payroll, profits, and national market activity
existing federal and state healthcare funding
targeted taxes on products with demonstrated public-health costs
savings from administrative consolidation and drug-price reform

layers.title: Pay rural systems for readiness
layers.summary: Community Health Readiness Budgets finance capacity like a fire department — not survival only by billing for illness. Expands beyond CAH/REH into a complete rural-capacity model.

layers.title: Invest heavily in primary care and prevention
layers.summary: Redirect a larger share of funding to the front door. Arkansas should create a protected Primary and Preventive Care Floor requiring a defined portion of Medicaid, public-employee, and regulated commercial-insurance spending for primary care and prevention — percentage requires modeling.

layers.title: Pay for outcomes without abandoning difficult communities
layers.summary: Value-based care must risk-adjust for poverty, rurality, housing, transportation, food access, disability, and provider scarcity — reward improvement without punishing inherited disadvantage.

rural_health_equity_formula.summary: Distribute funds by need rather than political influence or historical billing volume. Include a minimum community capacity payment.
rural_health_equity_formula.funding_principle: Equal citizenship does not always require identical spending. It requires enough capacity for every person to obtain a comparable basic standard of care.

community_health_network.transportation_rule: Transportation between levels is part of the healthcare system—not left entirely to the patient.

rural_workforce_pipeline.summary: Build the rural workforce locally through academy pathways beginning in local schools. Publicly funded professional education can be debt-free in exchange for defined underserved service — coordinated pipeline, not scattered small programs.

local_economic_engine.summary: Stable health networks create skilled jobs, purchasing power, workforce reliability, healthier children, support for aging residents, business recruitment, and emergency readiness — a central anchor for small-town implementation.

pharmaceutical_reform.summary: Preserve innovation while changing the relationship between public investment, pricing, and access.
reforms: full disclosure of research, manufacturing, marketing, and acquisition costs
faster lawful generic and biosimilar competition
outcome-based pricing for very expensive treatments
public manufacturing or nonprofit production where essential generic markets fail

insurance_reform.summary: Insurance should pool unpredictable risk — not profit primarily from confusion, denials, delay, or avoiding high-risk communities.
require: public reporting by county and income level

state_health_prosperity_fund.summary: Protected Arkansas fund for rural and underserved health capacity. Distribution follows the published rural-equity formula and appears in the People’s Ledger — not political favors.
revenue_examples: tobacco, vaping, and other evidence-based health-impact charges

prevention_dividend.summary: When a region reduces avoidable costs while maintaining quality, part of verified savings returns to that region for community health investments.

public_accountability.summary: Every county and health region publishes a public health dashboard. Private patient information remains protected; system performance does not.

federal: support for regions unable to maintain essential capacity alone

implementation_rule.text: Test regionally before statewide restructuring, with clearly defined costs, outcomes, failure triggers, and independent evaluation.

health_system_test.purpose: Screen healthcare finance, rural capacity, insurance, pharmaceutical, and prevention proposals.
questions: Does essential health security follow the person rather than an employer?
Does financing sustain low-population areas without punishing hiring or wages?
Are rural systems paid for readiness capacity, not illness volume alone?
Does the Rural Health Equity Formula allocate by need with a minimum capacity payment?
Is primary and preventive care protected by a meaningful spending floor?
Are outcomes risk-adjusted so difficult communities are not abandoned?
Does every resident connect to a Community Health Network with transportation between levels?
Is the workforce pipeline built locally with service-for-education pathways?
Do pharmaceutical and insurance rules preserve innovation while ending extraction through confusion or monopoly?
Are State Health Prosperity Fund and Prevention Dividend distributions public, formula-driven, and independently evaluated?
